title: Choose where your AI works.
description: A detailed comparison of Beans, OpenBot, Grok Bot, and Claude Code. Understand the workflow, model choices, data path, and real cost before you choose.
matrixBody: Twelve practical differences, based on the mechanisms described in each product’s documentation.
caption: Execution, models, tools, privacy, and costs
beansFit: You want named bots with direct model connections, group conversations, and encrypted pairing between computers and phones. You are comfortable keeping the assigned computer online.
costTitle: Separate the app from the AI bill.
costBody: Beans is free. That does not make model usage free. Each bot uses its connected provider, and parallel work can consume more allowance. A Runner needs to be online; using your own server also has operating costs.
startBody: Explore the actual desktop interface in the homepage demo, then check the published downloads for your device. The demo uses sample data and simulated replies, not a connected AI provider.

questions.q: Does encrypted sync mean the model cannot see my prompt?
questions.a: No. Device sync and model inference are separate. Beans encrypts data between paired devices, but your selected AI provider processes the content you send it to generate a reply.

questions.q: Can I keep my existing AI subscription?
questions.a: Beans offers ChatGPT and Grok subscription sign-in. Other built-in providers use API keys, and compatible servers have their own access requirements. Check your provider’s plan and usage rules.

questions.q: Does my phone run the bots?
questions.a: No. A paired phone is a chat device. Each bot runs on an assigned Mac, Windows, or Linux Runner. Work waits if that Runner is offline.
No. These pages compare documented mechanisms and workflows. They do not claim speed, quality, token savings, or reliability measurements.

freshness: Checked October 7, 2026. Product capabilities, availability, plans, and limits can change. Consult the linked official documentation before purchasing or migrating.

topics.title: Execution changes your everyday workflow.
topics.body: A Beans bot has one assigned Runner. It works in that computer’s folders with that computer’s user permissions. Choosing a local workspace or a managed cloud machine changes which files are available, what stays online, and who maintains the environment.

topics.title: Pick the provider without replacing the teammate.
topics.body: Beans stores a bot’s role separately from its model choice. Provider credentials belong to your account and sync encrypted to paired devices. A subscription login and an API key are different billing arrangements; having one does not automatically include the other.

topics.title: Collaboration is more than parallel windows.
topics.body: Beans has one-to-one chats and group chats with up to six bots. Mentions direct a turn to a bot, and handoffs pass work between teammates. Different Runners can contribute to the same chat, so the conversation can span your computers.

topics.title: Tools use the permissions you give them.
topics.body: Bots can work with files, execute commands, and use connected MCP tools. Review the app’s permission flows and the tools you install. Running a command with your user’s permissions is different from isolating it in an operating-system sandbox.

topics.title: Separate device privacy from model privacy.
topics.body: Beans encrypts account data before relay sync. The relay cannot decrypt the chat blobs. Inference still sends content to the model provider you choose. Review both the sync mechanism and that provider’s data policy when deciding what to share.

topics.title: Plan for work while you are away.
topics.body: Your phone lets you talk to bots on paired computers. It does not replace their Runner. Routines and new turns need the assigned computer online. For always-on work, choose a computer or server you can keep running and account for its maintenance.

openbot.intro: Both apps organize AI teammates. Beans connects models directly and pairs your devices with encrypted sync. OpenBot brings existing agent tools into a shared workspace, with local execution and an optional hosted server.
openbot.good: You want tools such as Codex or Claude Code inside a shared workspace, a built-in browser, or OpenBot’s optional hosted execution.
other: Local desktop; optional hosted server.

grok-bot.intro: Beans runs on a computer you assign. Grok Bot offers a managed computer that can continue working when your laptop is closed. The choice changes your operating responsibilities and how you connect tools.
grok-bot.good: You want a managed computer, bots that work while your laptop is closed, and access through an eligible Cursor or Grok plan.

claude-code.intro: Beans is a workspace for named bots across different jobs. Claude Code focuses on codebases, development commands, and coding sessions in the terminal, editor, desktop app, or web.
claude-code.good: Your main job is coding, and you want repository-oriented sessions, editor integrations, or Claude Code’s development tooling.
